goal: Teach Year-2 physics students to turn one familiar vertical-motion calculation into an ordered algorithm, trace a MATLAB for-loop, make one bounded parameter change, diagnose clear defects from evidence, and explain what validation does and does not prove.

deck_context.deck_context: Week 02 reuses the familiar one-dimensional vertical-launch model so the new cognitive load is algorithmic rather than mathematical. The lecture moves from prediction to one calculation, then to a repeatable recipe, index mapping, two-pass tracing, a MATLAB loop, bounded completion, controlled modification, plotted evidence, defect classification, validation limits, and transfer.
deck_context.core_claim: A loop becomes trustworthy when every pass has a clear input, current value, update, matching output slot, stopping point, check, and physical interpretation.
deck_context.locked_model: y(t) = y0 + v0 t - (1/2) g t^2; upward is positive; air resistance is neglected; gravity is constant; y0_m = 0 m; v0_mps = 20 m s^-1; g_mps2 = 9.81 m s^-2; t_s = 0:0.5:4 s.
deck_context.exactness: Equations, code, indices, numerical values, units, signs, assertions, and plot data are strict teaching content. Do not invent, paraphrase, or approximate them.

core: decompose into input, calculation, output, and check
modify one parameter and predict effect
stretch: write a reusable function from scratch

slides.title: One calculation is four small jobs
slides.intent: Give students the plain-language decomposition that makes a later loop understandable.
key_points: Input stores the model parameters and ordered times.
Calculate uses the current time in the model.
Store saves one position in the matching output slot.
Check compares the result with something already known.

slides.title: Turn the jobs into a repeatable recipe
slides.intent: Make loop vocabulary explicit in plain language before MATLAB punctuation.
key_points: Make one output slot for every input time.
Start at the first index.
Read the current time, calculate, and store one position.
Move to the next index and stop after the last.
slides.local_context: Render this exact six-step pseudocode: 1. Make one position slot per time; 2. Start at the first index; 3. Read the current time; 4. Calculate and store one position; 5. Move to the next index; 6. Stop after the last time. Highlight start, current, update, next, and stop.

slides.title: The index is a storage address, not a time
slides.intent: Connect MATLAB’s one-based index to a physical sample and matching output location.
key_points: MATLAB indexing starts at 1.
t_s(sample_index) selects the current physical time.
y_m(sample_index) selects the matching output slot.
The same index keeps input and output aligned.

slides.title: Trace two passes before trusting the whole loop
slides.intent: Demonstrate execution order with two concrete iterations before presenting the complete code.

The selected input and output location change together.
Trace symbols first; interpret the number physically second.

slides.title: Write the MATLAB loop that matches the recipe
slides.intent: Map the plain-language recipe onto a complete readable MATLAB loop.
key_points: Preallocate one position slot per time.
Loop from 1 to n_samples.
Use a scalar current_time_s inside the loop.
Store into the matching indexed output.
slides.local_context: Render this exact MATLAB code with line breaks: y_m = zeros(size(t_s)); / for sample_index = 1:n_samples /     current_time_s = t_s(sample_index); /     y_m(sample_index) = y0_m + v0_mps*current_time_s ... /         - 0.5*g_mps2*current_time_s^2; / end. Use numbered callouts 1 preallocate, 2 select, 3 calculate, 4 store. Keep ordinary * and ^ because current_time_s is scalar.

slides.title: Diagnose the defect before editing the code
slides.intent: Give students a decision path for distinguishing visible failure from plausible-but-wrong output.
key_points: Syntax defects stop MATLAB reading the intended structure.
Indexing or operator defects can run while storing or calculating the wrong thing.
Physical or logical defects can produce plausible numbers with wrong physics.
The code running is not a correctness test.
slides.local_context: Use exact short defect fragments and consequences: Syntax: for k = 1:numel(t_s); ...; % missing end -> MATLAB cannot determine the loop boundary. Indexing: y_m(1) = ... inside every loop pass -> code runs but overwrites one storage slot. Physical sign: y_m(k) = y0_m + v0_mps*t_s(k) + 0.5*g_mps2*t_s(k)^2 -> code runs but accelerates upward and contradicts upward-positive gravity. Evidence path: error location / pseudocode / output / physics.

slides.title: One check can pass while the model is still wrong
slides.intent: Show what a known-value check proves, what it misses, and why physical reasoning supplies a second check.
key_points: y(0) = 0 m is a known initial-value check.
assert(y_m(1) == y0_m) checks the first stored value.
A wrong gravity sign can still pass at t = 0.
Use the predicted trajectory as a second physical check.
slides.local_context: Use exact y(0) = 0 m and exact assertion assert(abs(y_m(1)-y0_m) < 1e-12). Show wrong-sign expression y_wrong(k) = y0_m + v0_mps*t_s(k) + 0.5*g_mps2*t_s(k)^2 and state initial check passes at t = 0; physical check fails because the ball accelerates upward. End with exact phrase check the number and the meaning.

Identify one defect and the evidence that reveals it.
